title: CHAPTER THIRTY-NINE. On the permission of sin, its foundation, opposite, connections, and consequences
english: CHAPTER THIRTY-NINE. On the permission of sin, and its foundation, opposite, connections, and consequences.

Thus far concerning sin: next follows its PERMISSION, which is an act of divine providence concerning it, by which all impediments that God knows would stop the sin if applied to human power or will, and also compelling forces that efficaciously drive toward doing what one abhors, are suspended. This locus on permission the most learned Twisse inquired into; Arminius also attempted it more than once. Ignorance of this doctrine makes it that when some could not understand whence sin is — inasmuch as it is the highest evil that is given, which cannot be from God who is most highly good — they denied Gods providence itself.

title: VI–III. What to weigh in permission; foundation in free choice and Gods wisdom and power
english: VI. In the permission of sin there is to be weighed its foundation, opposite, connections, and the consequences around the progress and consummation of sin. III. The foundation is partly the liberty of choice that God the creator planted in the rational creature, and whose use the Creator's constancy does not allow to be taken from that creature; partly Gods infinite wisdom and power, by which He knows and can produce good from evil.

Hence God permits whatever He permits: not unknowingly of creatures powers and affection, because He knows all things; not unwillingly, for He could have not produced a creature that would be of free choice, and could reduce one produced to nothing or change it in various ways.

title: IV–VIII. Opposite of permission: impediment and coercion; kinds of impediment
english: IV. The opposite of permission is impediment and coercion. Impediment is that by which an obstacle is set to the creatures power and will lest it sin. Coercion is that by which someone is efficaciously driven toward doing what he abhors. VI. By reason of efficiency it is either efficacious or inefficacious. VII. By reason of the object an impediment is set either to power or to will. VIII. An impediment set to power takes away the faculty; one set to will, without taking away the faculty, bends or holds it back. Permission is not a positive law of sin, nor is God the author of sin; but the suspension of impediments and the non-impeding of the act of a creature freely sinning.

title: XII–XVI. Connections of permission; direction of sin by providence
english: XII. Connected to permission in beginning, progress, and end are: foreknowledge, decree, ordination, direction, and determination. XVI. Direction is the divine providence by which the act of sin, though evil in itself, is directed by God toward good ends, whether toward an object or toward an end. Examples: Joseph sold by his brothers (Genesis 45:8); Job afflicted by Satan (Job 1-2); David and Absalom (2 Samuel 12; 15-16). God is said to do evils wrought by wicked humans and by Satan himself, because the chief parts in those actions by directing and determining were Gods, and because the power of harming effected no more than God determined.

title: XVIII–XX. Direction into object and end; determination of sin; Cap. 39 close
english: XVIII. Direction into an object is when God so moderates the sinners action that it falls on this object, not that — as He permitted David to resolve concerning Nabal, but did not permit him to pour out innocent blood (1 Samuel 25); He permitted him to flee to Achish and feign folly, but not to fight against Israel (1 Samuel 21; 27; 29). XIX. Direction into an end is when God draws from sin a good end, whether of justice or of mercy.

XX. Determination of sin is the act of providence by which God circumscribes the measure, time, mode, and limit of sin, lest it be able to rage beyond what He Himself wills (1 Corinthians 10:13; 2 Corinthians 4:8-9). Thus God by permitting does not cease to reign, nor does sin escape outside the limits of providence.
